Name: Institute for Replication (I4R)
Description: An ongoing initiative founded in 2022 and led by Abel Brodeur that systematically reproduces and replicates studies published in leading economics and political science journals, and has been expanding into psychology (through collaborations with Psychological Science and Nature Human Behaviour) as well as public health and ecology. Results are collated in a growing discussion paper series — more than 240 replication reports so far, many of them produced at the "replication games" the institute organizes around the world. Reports are written at the level of the paper and cover computational reproduction (re-running the original code and data), checks for coding errors, and robustness re-analyses that vary analytical decisions on the original data (e.g. changing control variables, samples, or estimation and inference methods); a smaller share of re-analyses introduce new data and so constitute replications in the stricter sense. Flagship result (Brodeur et al. 2026, Nature): across 110 articles (79 in economics, 31 in political science) from 12 leading journals with mandatory data- and code-sharing policies, over 85% of published claims were computationally reproducible, coding errors were found in about 25% of studies, and 72% of originally significant estimates remained statistically significant with the same sign under robustness re-analyses.
sampling_frame: Papers with available replication packages in leading economics and political science journals; aims for comprehensive coverage of partner journals
schema_source: Brodeur et al. 2026 Nature (10.1038/s41586-026-10251-x); I4R discussion paper series
exclusion_reason: Mostly computational reproduction and robustness re-analysis of the original authors' datasets, not new-data replication; no rows in our replications database (no tag)

Name: Social Science Reproduction Platform (SSRP)
Description: The Social Science Reproduction Platform, developed by the Berkeley Initiative for Transparency in the Social Sciences (BITSS) together with the American Economic Association's Data Editor, crowdsources and catalogs attempts to assess and improve the computational reproducibility of social science research, following a standardized reproduction protocol, and is widely used in teaching. It collates computational reproductions — re-running the original paper's data and code, what we call technical replications — rather than replications on new data.
sampling_frame: Crowdsourced; reproducers (often students in courses using the platform) choose which published papers and claims to reproduce
exclusion_reason: Computational reproduction of the original authors' data and code (technical replication), not new-data replication; no rows in our replications database (no tag)

Name: Does Empirical Finance Replicate? (Muravyev 2026)
Description: An LLM-driven attempt by Dmitriy Muravyev (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) to replicate the main result of every empirical paper published in the Journal of Finance, Journal of Financial Economics, and Review of Financial Studies from 2000 to 2020 (5,430 articles screened). An autonomous LLM pipeline (building on Andrew Chen's harness) identifies the key coefficients behind each paper's main result, rebuilds the sample from available databases (CRSP, Compustat and similar), and re-estimates the coefficients first in the original sample period (a reproduction) and then in the years after the sample ends (an out-of-sample test on new data); independent LLM auditors check each implementation before seeing the estimates, and closeness to the published values is scored by fixed formulas. Theoretical papers and papers needing confidential, hand-collected, or unavailable commercial data were excluded, leaving 1,328 in-sample replications, 1,005 of them with enough later data for an out-of-sample test. In sample, 75% of papers reproduce the published sign and significance and the median coefficient ratio is 0.93; out of sample, the rate falls to 42% (48% after adjusting for precision) and the median coefficient ratio to 0.45. The coefficient ratio drops sharply at the end of the original sample and is flat on either side, which the author reads as consistent with data snooping rather than investor learning or gradual market change; standard publication-selection models explain only about one-fifth of the decay. Results from the lower-ranked Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis (268 papers) reproduce as well in sample (74%) but decay more out of sample (33%, median ratio 0.34). Replication packages for 205 of the most-cited papers, including failed replications, are posted at dmurav.com/replications. Individual failures may reflect substitute data, database vintages, or reconstruction errors rather than errors in the original paper.
sampling_frame: All empirical articles in the Journal of Finance, Journal of Financial Economics and Review of Financial Studies, 2000-2020, whose main result can be rebuilt from available databases (plus JFQA 2000-2020 as a comparison sample)
success_criterion: same sign and statistical significance (category match), plus coefficient ratio
exclusion_reason: Automated (LLM) reconstruction from standard databases rather than new-data replication of the original study; out-of-sample tests use later years of the same databases; no rows in our replications database (no tag)
